text: Here is an array of eight numbers, already in sorted order.
Sorted is the one thing that binary search absolutely insists on.
We want to find the value seven, if it is here at all.
We begin with a search window covering the entire array.
Lo marks the first cell, and hi marks one past the last.
We will count every comparison, to see how few we need.
Rather than scanning, jump straight to the middle, at index four.
The value waiting there is nine, and we are hunting for seven.
Nine is too big, so seven cannot possibly be to its right.
So hi drops to four, and half the array is discarded.
One comparison just eliminated four of the eight cells.
Take the middle of what survives, which is index two.
The value there is four, which is smaller than seven.
Four is too small, so seven cannot be to its left.
Lo climbs to three, and the window is down to one cell.
Two comparisons, and a single candidate is all that remains.
The middle of a one cell window is that cell itself.
And the value sitting there is exactly seven.
That is our target, found in only three comparisons.
Binary search reports index three, and stops right there.
Look at how the window shrank: eight, then four, then one.
Every comparison throws away half of whatever is left.
Three comparisons for eight cells, because two cubed is eight.
Double the array to sixteen, and it costs just one more probe.
In general, the cost is the logarithm of n, base two.
A linear scan would have to walk the cells one at a time.
All that speed is bought with one requirement: the array must be sorted.
Sort once, and then find anything in just a handful of steps.
